title: National Credit Union Administration v. First National Bank & Trust Co.
shortTitle: National Credit Union Administration v. First National Bank & Trust Co.
summary: Bank competitors fell within the arguable zone of interests of a statutory common-bond limitation on credit unions, and the Court rejected NCUA’s interpretation permitting unrelated employer groups.
notes: The zone-of-interests test 'does not require any indication of congressional purpose to benefit the would-be plaintiff'; the Court also held at Chevron step one that the common-bond provision unambiguously applied to every member of a credit union, not just each employer group (5-4, Thomas, J.).

sections.Parties: Five banks and the American Bankers Association challenged the National Credit Union Administration’s approval of expanded credit-union membership. AT&T Family Federal Credit Union and the Credit Union National Association intervened as defendants and joined the agency’s side. The banks asserted injury from competition for customers.
sections.Material Facts: The Federal Credit Union Act limited membership to groups with a common occupational or associational bond, or groups within a defined community. Until 1982 the agency required one occupational bond across a credit union’s members. It then permitted multiple unrelated employer groups, each internally sharing a bond. AT&T’s credit union expanded to about 110,000 members, with only 35 percent employed by AT&T or affiliates. The banks challenged 1990 charter amendments adding unrelated groups. Competitive injury in fact was undisputed; the issue was whether the banks’ interest also fell within the statute’s zone.
sections.Procedural History: The district court initially dismissed for lack of prudential standing. The D.C. Circuit reversed. On remand, the district court upheld the interpretation under Chevron, and the court of appeals again reversed. The Supreme Court affirmed the appellate result, addressing both the statutory threshold and the interpretation. Justice Thomas wrote the majority; Scalia declined to join footnote 6’s reliance on legislative history. O’Connor dissented with Stevens, Souter, and Breyer.
sections.Issue: Whether commercial-bank competitors were within the arguable zone of interests protected by the common-bond provision and whether the agency permissibly interpreted that provision to allow unrelated employer groups.
sections.Holding: The banks could obtain APA review, and the challenged interpretation was impermissible. The common-bond limitation arguably protected an interest in restricting the customer markets credit unions could serve, which matched the banks’ competitive interest. The source summarizes the merits ruling as resting on Congress’s unambiguous contrary intent; the judgment was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: The majority rejected a demand for proof that Congress specifically meant to benefit these bank plaintiffs. It identified an objective connection: membership limits restrict customers because credit unions generally serve members. Banks injured by expansion therefore asserted an interest within the statutory zone. Air Courier differed because postal employees’ job concerns did not match the relevant monopoly statute’s revenue and service interests. O’Connor argued that the majority described the interest so broadly that any party with injury from nonenforcement would qualify. In her reading, the common-bond requirement governed financial stability and internal cooperative relationships, and its incidental effects on competitors did not establish a protected competitive interest. She stressed the distinction between the statute’s intended interests and whoever would benefit from enforcement. The excerpt supplies the complete standing dispute but only a short editorial summary of the Chevron merits analysis; the account therefore preserves that boundary.
